title: Redline
full_review:
At heart a teenage drag-race movie in the old Hollywood style, the mindless "Redline" (Chicago Pictures) is a self-financed production from real-estate mogul Daniel Sadek, starring his collection of exotic sports cars as well as his ex-fiancee.

The latter, Nadja Bjorlin, plays Natasha "Nat" Martin, a glamorous tomboy who customizes sports cars alongside her widowed, mechanic mom (Barbara Niven).

After one of her clients, music mogul Infamous (comedian Eddie Griffin), accompanies her on a hair-raising test run of his performance-enhanced wheels, he recruits her as his driver in a series of high-stakes, illegal road races.

His fellow high rollers -- primarily movie producer Jerry Brecken (Tim Matheson) and eccentric, philosophical hedonist Michael D'orizio (Angus Macfadyen) -- stake millions on each race, generally held on regular roads and streets. The minimal plot concerns war hero Carlo ((Nathan Philips) avenging the racing death of his brother, Jason (Jesse Johnson), by attempting to kill their uncle, Michael, and rescuing the kidnapped Nat along the way. But the movie is just an unabashed excuse to show off fantasy cars revving through their paces.

Directed by Andy Cheng, a stunt coordinator and second-unit director, it has a style halfway between a music video and a video game. Ultimately chaste and containing violence about on a par with a 1970s TV cop show, the film's celebration of Dionysian lifestyles and materialistic excess is regrettable.

The film contains some crude and crass language; mild sexual innuendo; an excessive amount of skimpily dressed women, though no nudity; some bloodless fight scenes; shots fired and explosions; and two killings. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
